Taipei's public library system has begun piloting a small number of branches that stay open until two in the morning during exam season, responding to years of requests from university students and senior-high students preparing for entrance exams. The pilot branches, located near several major universities, report that seats fill up almost entirely by ten each evening, with many students bringing snacks and blankets to settle in for the long night ahead.

Library staff say the extended hours required more than simply keeping the lights on. Security guards now work overnight shifts, and a rotating team of librarians remains on duty to answer questions and enforce a strict quiet policy, since a single loud conversation can disturb dozens of focused students in a shared reading room.

Not everyone supports the change. Some neighbourhood residents worry that a brightly lit, all-night library will attract noise and litter to a quiet residential street. Library officials respond that entrances are monitored by camera and that similar programmes in other cities have not caused the problems residents fear.

For now, the library plans to continue the pilot through the end of the academic year before deciding whether to expand the programme to additional branches across the city.

Several office towers in downtown Taipei have installed beehives on their rooftops over the past three years, joining a growing number of cities worldwide experimenting with urban beekeeping. Building managers say the hives were originally installed mostly as a marketing gesture, a way to advertise environmental responsibility to tenants, but many have been surprised by how effective the bees turn out to be at pollinating nearby rooftop gardens and balcony plants.

Maintaining a rooftop hive is not as simple as setting up a box and walking away. A trained beekeeper visits each site roughly twice a month to check the health of the colony, harvest honey when appropriate, and make sure the bees are not becoming aggressive toward people using the rooftop terrace. Office workers are generally kept a safe distance from the hives themselves, though some buildings now offer occasional tours for curious employees.

The honey produced is often given to tenants as a small gift or sold at reduced prices in the building lobby, with proceeds sometimes donated to environmental education programmes. Beekeepers involved in these projects note that urban honey can taste noticeably different from rural honey, since city bees draw nectar from an unusually wide mix of flowering plants found in nearby parks and gardens.

For generations, farmers across Taiwan have relied on experience and intuition to decide when to harvest crops ahead of an approaching typhoon, often guessing wrong and losing an entire season's income in a single storm. A newly developed smartphone app aims to replace some of that guesswork with hyperlocal weather data drawn from a dense network of government sensors and satellite imagery.

Unlike general weather forecasts, which cover broad regions, the app generates predictions specific to a farmer's exact field location, factoring in local wind patterns, elevation, and soil drainage. It sends alerts recommending whether to harvest early, reinforce greenhouse structures, or simply wait, along with an estimated confidence level for each recommendation.

During its first full typhoon season, farmers using the app reported harvesting an average of eighteen hours earlier than they otherwise would have, giving them a meaningful head start before the worst winds and rain arrived. Developers acknowledge the app is not perfect; predictions become significantly less reliable more than three days before a storm's expected arrival, and farmers in mountainous areas report that local terrain sometimes causes unexpected forecast errors.

Agricultural officials are now considering offering the app free of charge to all registered farms, hoping that fewer weather-related losses will ultimately mean more stable food prices for consumers nationwide.

On the first Saturday of every month, a community centre in New Taipei City transforms into something between a workshop and a social gathering: a repair cafe, where volunteers with skills in electronics, sewing, and small appliance repair help neighbours fix broken belongings for free. Visitors bring in anything from a wobbly chair to a toaster that no longer heats, and volunteers work alongside them rather than simply doing the repair themselves.

The format is intentional. Organisers want visitors to leave not just with a fixed item, but with enough understanding to attempt similar repairs on their own next time. This hands-on approach occasionally means a repair takes longer than a professional shop would need, but volunteers argue that the extra time spent teaching is the entire point of the event.

Repair cafes have grown steadily in popularity as households become more aware of the environmental cost of constantly replacing broken items rather than mending them. Electronic waste in particular has become a growing concern, since many small appliances are difficult to recycle safely and often end up in landfills.

Not every item can be saved. Volunteers are honest when something is beyond repair, and they encourage visitors to consider this outcome as useful information rather than a failure, since it at least prevents unnecessary spending on a doomed repair attempt.

Every Thursday evening, a small community radio station in Miaoli broadcasts an hour-long programme conducted almost entirely in Hakka, a language that UNESCO has classified as vulnerable due to declining numbers of fluent younger speakers. The show's host, a retired schoolteacher named Ah-Mei, mixes traditional Hakka folk songs with call-in segments where listeners share family stories and childhood memories in the language.

Ah-Mei never expected the programme to attract much of an audience beyond elderly residents who grew up speaking Hakka at home. She has been surprised, however, by a steady trickle of younger listeners, many of whom say they understand more Hakka than they can comfortably speak, having grown up hearing grandparents use it without ever needing to respond in kind.

To reach this generation more directly, the station recently began posting show segments online with Mandarin subtitles, hoping that listeners uncertain of certain words could follow along and gradually build confidence. Ah-Mei is realistic about what a single radio programme can accomplish; she does not expect it to reverse decades of declining Hakka fluency by itself.

Still, she says the messages she receives from younger listeners, some admitting they called their grandparents in Hakka for the first time in years after hearing the show, convince her the effort is worthwhile, even if the language's long-term survival remains genuinely uncertain.
